bodyMarkdown:
## The idea in plain language

Area is how much paint you need to cover a shape. Perimeter is how much fence you need around it. They are completely different quantities, and two shapes with the same perimeter can have wildly different areas — a long thin rectangle versus a square, for instance.

Most exam questions are one standard shape, or a standard shape with a piece added or removed.

## What is actually going on

Learn the handful of standard formulas, then treat every complicated figure as standard shapes **added together or subtracted from each other**. A path around a garden is the big rectangle minus the small one. A shaded region is usually one shape with another cut out.

One relationship worth internalising: scaling every length by $k$ multiplies the perimeter by $k$ but the area by $k^2$. Doubling a room's dimensions quadruples the carpet needed.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: A rectangular garden 20 m by 15 m is surrounded by a 2 m wide path on the outside. Find the area of the path.
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
The path adds 2 m on **each** side, so the outer rectangle is $20 + 4 = 24$ m by $15 + 4 = 19$ m.

Outer area $= 24 \times 19 = 456$ square m.
Garden area $= 20 \times 15 = 300$ square m.

Path area $= 456 - 300 = 156$ square m.
workedExamples.altSolutionMarkdown: Adding 2 m only once to each dimension is the classic error — the path runs along both sides.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: Find the area of a circle inscribed in a square of side 14 cm. Use $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$.
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
An inscribed circle touches all four sides, so its diameter equals the square's side.

Diameter 14, so radius 7.

Area $= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 49 = 154$ square cm.

formulaCards.title: Standard areas
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: Rectangle $lb$. Triangle $\dfrac12 bh$. Circle $\pi r^2$. Trapezium $\dfrac12(a+b)h$. Parallelogram $bh$.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: A trapezium with parallel sides 8 and 12 and height 5 has area 50.

formulaCards.title: Perimeters
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: A square of side 9 has perimeter 36 and area 81.

formulaCards.title: Scaling
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: Multiplying every length by $k$ multiplies perimeter by $k$ and area by $k^2$.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: Tripling the side of a square makes the area nine times larger.

commonTraps: Adding a border width only once per dimension instead of twice.
Confusing radius and diameter in circle formulas.
Mixing units — metres with centimetres — inside one calculation.
